clips.title: Join Hierarchy: Theta, Equi, Natural
clips.hook: Join as cross product plus selection, and how theta, equi and self joins relate, with renaming.
clips.summary: Join is a compound operator: cross product followed by selection on theta. Theta joins generalize equi-joins (conjunction of equalities). A self join with a predicate like age1 < age2 yields the cross-product schema, so duplicate column names need renaming.

quiz.question: In a self join S ⋈_{age1 < age2} S, what is the schema of the result before renaming?
options: Only columns satisfying the predicate
Same as a natural join: duplicate columns projected away
Same as the cross product: all columns of both copies, with duplicate names
Only the columns of one copy of S
quiz.explanation: A theta join is a cross product followed by selection; selection does not change the schema, so columns are duplicated and need renaming.

clips.title: Subnet Mask and Default Gateway: Choosing the Next-Hop
clips.hook: How a host uses mask and gateway config to decide which destination MAC to put in a frame.
clips.summary: The IP packet keeps end-to-end source and destination IPs, but the Ethernet header's destination MAC must be a node on the local link. A /24 mask (24 ones) tells the host which prefixes are on-link. Anything else goes to the configured default gateway, whose MAC becomes the frame destination.
clips.videoTitle: ARP: Mapping between IP and Ethernet | Networking tutorial (9 of 13)

quiz.question: Host A (192.168.9.2/24) sends a packet to 192.168.20.2. What are the destination IP and the destination MAC of the Ethernet frame?
options: Dest IP 192.168.20.2; dest MAC of host B
Dest IP 192.168.20.2; dest MAC of the router (gateway)
Dest IP 192.168.9.1; dest MAC of the router
Dest IP 192.168.20.2; broadcast MAC
quiz.explanation: The destination IP stays end-to-end. The destination isn't in the /24, so the frame is addressed at layer 2 to the default gateway's MAC.

clips.title: Non-pipelined divider: structural hazard and stalls
clips.hook: Why hardware detects and stalls on a busy divider instead of pipelining it.
clips.summary: Because the divider is not pipelined, a second divide must stall in decode until the divider frees. Pipelining or duplicating dividers costs much hardware and divisions are rare, so it is not cost-effective; compilers schedule other work in between.

quiz.question: Why do designers usually not pipeline or replicate the divider to remove its structural hazard?
options: Pipelined dividers violate precise exceptions
Register file has too few read ports
Division results cannot be forwarded
High hardware cost for a rarely used operation
quiz.explanation: Extra hardware would be mostly idle since divisions are rare, so detect-and-stall plus compiler scheduling is more cost-effective.

clips.title: Register-file write port conflicts in multi-latency pipelines
clips.hook: Three instructions can reach write-back in the same cycle; why the MEM stage often prevents it.
clips.summary: With different latencies, multiple instructions (e.g. mul, add, load) may target write-back in the same cycle. Fixes are stalling or adding write ports (more complex register file); in practice the serializing MEM stage makes the contrived case impossible.

quiz.question: What are the two ways to resolve several instructions wanting to write the register file in the same cycle?
options: Flush, or add read ports
Stall, or add write ports
Reorder, or add cache
Forward, or rename
quiz.explanation: Either serialize via stalls or have n write ports allowing n writes per cycle.

clips.title: WAW hazards and the busy-bit solution
clips.hook: How a shorter-latency add can write a register before an earlier multiply, and how busy bits stop it.
clips.summary: A later short-latency instruction can write a register before an earlier long-latency one, leaving a stale value for later readers. Stall in decode if the destination has a pending write, using a busy bit set at decode and cleared at write-back; since such code is rare, this simple scheme suffices.

quiz.question: How does the busy-bit scheme prevent a WAW hazard?
options: Set in WB, cleared in decode
Set in fetch, cleared in MEM
Set in decode, cleared in write-back; stall issue if destination is busy
Forward the later result to the earlier instruction
quiz.explanation: An instruction whose destination is already marked busy is not issued until the earlier write completes.

clips.title: RAW stalls in long pipelines: a dependent chain
clips.hook: Trace a load→mul→add→store chain and count the stalls in a multi-cycle FP pipeline.
clips.summary: A dependent chain load→multiply→add→store incurs many stalls: load-use, waiting for the 6-stage multiplier, and fetch/decode stalls propagating back since each stage holds one instruction. The store has an extra stall because MEM serializes it with the add.

quiz.question: Why does the add stall in IF as well as ID when the multiply is stalled?
options: Structural hazard on memory
Fetch needs the register file
Branch prediction
Only one instruction can occupy ID at a time
quiz.explanation: A stalled instruction in ID blocks the following instruction in IF.

clips.title: Forwarding complexity with multiple execution pipelines
clips.hook: Why forwarding needs huge muxes and comparators with several long pipelines.
clips.summary: Every FP instruction's source registers must be compared with destinations in many pipeline registers (end of each execution unit, MEM, WB). Large multiplexers in front of each unit select between register-file values and many forwarded results, greatly increasing wiring and logic over the 5-stage pipeline.

quiz.question: What does forwarding in a multi-pipeline design require at each functional unit input?
options: A large mux over register-file value and results from many pipeline registers, plus destination comparators
Only more write ports
A single 2:1 mux
A busy bit per stage
quiz.explanation: Results can come from the ends of several execution pipelines, so muxes and comparisons scale up.

clips.title: Default Initialization: Type and Storage Duration
clips.hook: Why a local int is indeterminate but a static int is zero, and how std::string differs.
clips.summary: Default initialization occurs with no initializer and depends on type and storage duration. Local primitives are indeterminate (reading is UB), class types invoke the default constructor, and static/global objects are zero-initialized first.

quiz.question: Given `void f(){ int a; static int d; std::string b; }`, which statement is correct?
options: d is indeterminate because int is primitive
b is zero-initialized then never constructed
Reading a is UB; d is zero-initialized; b is empty via its default constructor
Reading a is well-defined and yields 0
quiz.explanation: Automatic primitives are indeterminate (UB to read); statics get zero-initialization; class types run their default constructor.

clips.title: Value Initialization and the Vexing Parse
clips.hook: How empty braces zero-initialize before constructors and why parentheses can declare a function.
clips.summary: Value initialization with empty initializer yields zero/empty values appropriate to the type. For classes with default constructors, members may be zero-initialized before the constructor runs. Empty parentheses on a declaration would parse as a function declaration, so braces are required.

quiz.question: Why must `int var1{};` use braces rather than `int var1();` for value initialization in a declaration?
options: Braces are required for all primitives
Parentheses call the copy constructor
`int var1();` is parsed as a function declaration
Parentheses cause default initialization to leave it indeterminate
quiz.explanation: The most vexing parse treats `int var1();` as declaring a function returning int.

clips.title: List vs Direct Initialization: vector{5,10} vs vector(5,10)
clips.hook: Why replacing parentheses with braces silently changes std::vector semantics.
clips.summary: List initialization prefers an initializer_list constructor, falling back to matching constructors, else a compile error. So vector<int>{5,10} has two elements 5 and 10, while vector<int>(5,10) has five elements of value 10... the transcript's example gives count then value, so sizes and contents differ. Blind search-and-replace of parentheses with braces changes behavior.

quiz.question: What is the overload resolution preference for `std::vector<int> x{5,10};`?
options: initializer_list constructor, giving elements 5 and 10
Compile error from ambiguity
Constructor (count, value)
Copy constructor
quiz.explanation: List initialization first considers initializer_list constructors, so x has elements 5 and 10.

clips.title: Adam: Momentum + RMSprop with Bias Correction
clips.hook: Walk through the full Adam update: two moving averages, bias correction, and the combined step.
clips.summary: Adam keeps an EMA of gradients (v, beta1) and an EMA of squared gradients (s, beta2), bias-corrects both by 1-beta^t, and updates W by alpha * v_hat / (sqrt(s_hat)+eps). It combines momentum's direction smoothing with RMSprop's per-parameter scaling.

quiz.question: In Adam, what is the role of dividing v by (1 - beta1^t) and s by (1 - beta2^t)?
options: It normalizes gradients to unit length
It corrects the bias of the zero-initialized moving averages toward zero in early iterations
It decays the learning rate over time
It prevents division by zero in the denominator
quiz.explanation: Since v and s start at 0, early EMAs are underestimates; dividing by 1 - beta^t removes this initialization bias.

clips.title: Adam Hyperparameters and Why It's Called Adaptive Moment Estimation
clips.hook: Defaults for beta1, beta2, epsilon, and how first and second moments give Adam its name.
clips.summary: Defaults are beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, epsilon=1e-8; mainly alpha is tuned. beta1 estimates the first moment (mean of gradients) and beta2 the second moment (mean of squared gradients), hence adaptive moment estimation.

quiz.question: Which quantity does the beta2 moving average estimate in Adam?
options: The Hessian diagonal
The mean of the squared gradients (second moment)
The mean of the gradients (first moment)
The learning rate schedule
quiz.explanation: beta2 averages element-wise squared gradients, the (uncentered) second moment.

clips.title: Merge join: sort both inputs, then one linear scan
clips.hook: How sorting on the join key lets two relations be joined in a single sequential pass.
clips.summary: Both relations are sorted on the join attribute, then scanned together like merging sorted lists. Once the key changes, all rows for the previous key are known to be processed, so there is no rescanning. The cost is the up-front sort, and indexes can skip that sort.
clips.videoTitle: How nested loop, hash, and merge joins work.

quiz.question: In a sort-merge join, why can the scan advance past a join key once the keys stop matching?
options: Because the right table is always smaller
Because the hash of that key has been cached
Because an index guarantees uniqueness of the key
Because both inputs are sorted, so all rows with that key are contiguous and already consumed
quiz.explanation: Sorting groups equal keys together, so when the key changes no later row can match the earlier key.

clips.title: Hash join: build, probe, and its memory/skew costs
clips.hook: Build a hash table on one input, probe with the other, and see why it only fits equi-joins.
clips.summary: One table is hashed on the join attribute (build phase), then the other is scanned and probed. Collisions require rechecking the actual join key. It suits equi-joins only, needs extra memory, and degrades if the hash distribution is skewed.
clips.videoTitle: How nested loop, hash, and merge joins work.

quiz.question: Why must a hash join still compare join keys after finding a matching hash bucket?
options: Hash tables are unsorted
Different keys can collide into the same bucket
Buckets store only row IDs
The probe table may contain NULLs only
quiz.explanation: Collisions put different keys in one slot, so the equality predicate must be verified.

clips.title: ARP Target Is the Next Hop, Not the Destination
clips.hook: Why a host ARPs for the default gateway when the destination IP is on a foreign network.
clips.summary: If the destination is on the same subnet, the host ARPs for the destination IP. If it is on a foreign network, the host ARPs for its default gateway's IP instead. The gateway's MAC is then cached and used for all off-subnet traffic.
clips.videoTitle: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) in less than 5 minutes

quiz.question: Host B (10.3.3.x) sends a packet to a host on another network. Which IP address does B ARP for?
options: The router's IP on the remote network
The broadcast address of the subnet
The default gateway's IP
The remote destination host's IP
quiz.explanation: ARP only resolves addresses on the local link. For off-subnet destinations, the frame is addressed to the default gateway's MAC, so B ARPs for the gateway's IP.

clips.title: Anatomy of a Branch Predictor: Direction vs Target
clips.hook: Why fetch-stage prediction needs a direction predictor plus a BTB, and static policies' trade-offs.
clips.summary: Prediction must happen in fetch, before decode, so it splits into a branch-identification/target problem (BTB) and a direction problem (direction predictor). Always-not-taken needs neither structure (~30-40% accurate); always-taken needs only a BTB (~60-70%, good for backward loop branches).

quiz.question: Why does an always-taken static predictor require a BTB but no direction predictor?
options: The BTB stores the direction bit
Taken branches need a larger cache
Direction is always known from the opcode, but the target address must be supplied at fetch
The BTB is needed to detect mispredictions
quiz.explanation: Direction is fixed (taken), so no direction predictor is needed, but the target must be available in fetch, which the BTB provides.

clips.title: Defaulted Constructors: In-Class vs Out-of-Class
clips.hook: Why '= default' outside the class makes a constructor user-provided, and why it matters for const objects.
clips.summary: A constructor defaulted on its first declaration is not user-provided; defaulting it out of class makes it user-provided, though the implementation is identical. Since const default-initialization requires a user-provided default constructor, this matters, although compilers mostly don't enforce it. An empty body {} is a portable fix.

quiz.question: Why can `const MyClassB obj;` be well-formed when MyClassB's default constructor is declared `= default` outside the class, per the standard?
options: Out-of-class defaulting makes the constructor virtual
Const objects never need constructors
The compiler zero-initializes all const objects regardless
Out-of-class defaulting makes the constructor user-provided, which the rule for const default-initialization requires
quiz.explanation: Defaulting at first declaration is not user-provided; defaulting out of class is, which satisfies the const default-initialization rule.

clips.title: Copy Constructor: Shallow Copy and the Destructor Rule
clips.hook: What the implicit copy constructor does, why it breaks with owning pointers, and the deprecation rule.
clips.summary: The implicit copy constructor memberwise-copies bases and members, so pointers are shallow-copied and both objects share the pointee. If you need a destructor to free resources, you likely need a custom copy constructor; implicit copy generation is deprecated when a destructor is declared but still works.

quiz.question: A class owns a raw pointer freed in its destructor and relies on the implicit copy constructor. What is the likely problem?
options: The pointee is deep copied twice
Both copies point to the same memory, causing double free
Compile error because copy is deleted
The move constructor is called instead
quiz.explanation: Memberwise copy copies the pointer value, so both destructors free the same allocation.

clips.title: Move Constructor and Implicit Generation Rules
clips.hook: Moved-from state and when the compiler suppresses the implicit move constructor.
clips.summary: A move constructor takes T&&, leaving the source valid only for destruction or assignment unless the type promises more (e.g. unique_ptr becomes null). Declaring a copy constructor, copy assignment, move assignment or destructor suppresses the implicit move constructor, so the class falls back to copy or is not movable if copy is deleted.

quiz.question: A class explicitly deletes its copy constructor and declares no move constructor. What is true?
options: The class is neither copyable nor movable
Copy is deleted but move falls back to copy
Move constructor is implicitly generated
Compiler error at class definition
quiz.explanation: Declaring the copy constructor suppresses implicit move, so move requests find no viable move constructor and the deleted copy constructor is selected.

clips.title: Copy/Move Assignment and the By-Value Parameter Pitfall
clips.hook: How assignment differs from construction, and what happens when operator= takes its parameter by value.
clips.summary: Assignment operates on an existing object, while constructors create a new one. Copy assignment must have exactly one parameter. A by-value parameter invokes the copy constructor first, which is the basis of copy-and-swap; the move assignment takes an rvalue reference and leaves the source unusable.

quiz.question: What happens when a user-defined copy assignment operator takes its parameter by value?
options: It's not allowed to compile
The argument is copy-constructed before the body runs
It becomes a move assignment
It is called twice
quiz.explanation: Pass-by-value copy-constructs the parameter from the argument first.

clips.title: Why a Fixed Learning Rate Stalls in Mini-Batch SGD
clips.hook: Mini-batch gradient noise stops convergence with fixed alpha; decaying alpha shrinks the oscillation region.
clips.summary: With small mini-batches, gradient estimates are noisy, so a constant alpha makes iterates wander around the minimum instead of converging. Large alpha early gives fast progress, and shrinking alpha later confines the iterates to a tighter region around the minimum.

quiz.question: Why does mini-batch gradient descent with a fixed learning rate fail to converge exactly to a minimum?
options: The loss function is non-convex, so no minimum exists
A fixed alpha makes the Hessian singular
Gradient noise from different mini-batches keeps perturbing updates by a non-vanishing amount scaled by alpha
Mini-batches always produce biased gradients that point away from the minimum
quiz.explanation: Each mini-batch gradient is a noisy estimate. With constant alpha the update noise does not vanish, so iterates fluctuate around the minimum. Decaying alpha reduces the noise-induced step size.

clips.title: Inverse-Time Decay: alpha = alpha0 / (1 + decay_rate · epoch)
clips.hook: Work through the 1/(1+k·epoch) schedule and see how decay rate and alpha0 are hyperparameters.
clips.summary: The learning rate is set per epoch as alpha = alpha0 / (1 + decay_rate · epoch_num), which adds the decay rate as a hyperparameter to tune together with alpha0. With alpha0 = 0.2 and decay rate 1, alpha is 0.1, about 0.067, 0.05 and 0.04 over epochs 1 to 4. The speaker states the later values as 0.67, 0.5 and 0.4, which are off by a factor of 10.

quiz.question: With alpha0 = 0.2 and decay_rate = 1 in alpha = alpha0/(1 + decay_rate·epoch), what is alpha at epoch 3?

clips.title: Other Decay Schedules: Exponential, Sqrt, and Staircase
clips.hook: Compare exponential, 1/sqrt, and discrete-step schedules for decaying the learning rate.
clips.summary: Exponential decay uses alpha = 0.95^epoch · alpha0, which shrinks alpha geometrically. Other options scale alpha0 by k/sqrt(epoch) or k/sqrt(t), where t is the mini-batch number, or use a staircase that halves alpha at discrete intervals. Each choice brings its own hyperparameters.

quiz.question: Which schedule decays the learning rate fastest asymptotically?
options: Exponential: 0.95^epoch · alpha0
They all decay at the same rate
Inverse-time: alpha0/(1+k·epoch)
k/sqrt(epoch) · alpha0
quiz.explanation: Geometric decay falls faster than polynomial decay such as 1/epoch or 1/sqrt(epoch) as epochs grow.

clips.title: Derived-table join for above-department-average salary
clips.hook: Why per-group aggregates need a join back, solved with an independent subquery as a derived table.
clips.summary: A row-level comparison against a group aggregate needs the aggregate alongside each row. Compute AVG(salary) GROUP BY dept_id in a subquery used as a virtual table, join it on department ID, then filter salary > avg.
clips.videoTitle: Independent vs Correlated Subquery | Advanced SQL Tutorial For Beginners

quiz.question: To find employees earning more than their department average using an independent subquery, why is a join needed?
options: GROUP BY cannot be used with WHERE
AVG cannot be computed without a join
Joins are faster than WHERE conditions
The per-department average must be attached to each employee row before comparing
quiz.explanation: The aggregate lives in a different row set (one row per department); joining on dept ID attaches it to each employee row so a WHERE salary > avg can filter.

clips.title: What makes a subquery independent
clips.hook: Two properties: it executes standalone, and it is evaluated once.
clips.summary: An independent subquery has no references to the outer query, so it can be run on its own. It is evaluated once and its result is used by the outer query.
clips.videoTitle: Independent vs Correlated Subquery | Advanced SQL Tutorial For Beginners

clips.title: 1D vs 2D Parity: Detection Power and Single-Bit Correction
clips.hook: How a grid of row/column parity bits detects two-bit errors and locates single-bit errors.
clips.summary: Single parity detects any odd number of bit errors but misses even counts. Two-dimensional parity adds row and column parity bits, which always detects two-bit errors and, for a single flip, locates the bit at the intersection of the failing row and column.

quiz.question: In a 2D even-parity scheme, the receiver finds a parity failure in row 2 and column 3 only. What is the most likely conclusion?
options: Two bits flipped in row 2
The bit at (row 2, column 3) flipped and can be corrected
The parity bits themselves were lost, so retransmit
The frame has no errors
quiz.explanation: A single flip toggles exactly one row parity and one column parity; their intersection identifies the flipped bit, so it can be corrected without retransmission.

clips.title: CRC: Computing R by Modulo-2 Division
clips.hook: Why CRC bits are the remainder of D·2^r divided by G, and why it detects bursts.
clips.summary: The sender picks r CRC bits so that D·2^r XOR R is exactly divisible by generator G (r+1 bits). XORing R on both sides shows R is the remainder of D·2^r divided by G. The receiver divides and flags a nonzero remainder, and CRC detects all bursts shorter than r+1 bits.

quiz.question: In CRC with generator G of r+1 bits, how does the sender obtain R?
options: R = parity of D
R = sum of the bytes of D in one's complement
R = D XOR G
R = remainder of (D·2^r) divided by G, using modulo-2 arithmetic
quiz.explanation: D·2^r XOR R divisible by G implies R = (D·2^r) mod G, so appending R makes the whole frame divisible by G.

clips.title: Why Mispredictions Cost 20–100 Cycles
clips.hook: How fetch PC dependence on branch direction/target forces speculation, and why flushes are so costly.
clips.summary: The next fetch PC depends on branch direction and target, unknown until decode or execute, so stalling wastes cycles proportional to pipeline depth. Predicting lets fetch speculate, but a wrong guess flushes the pipeline, costing 20 to nearly 100 cycles on Pentium 4, and branches occur every 5 to 20 instructions.

quiz.question: Why does the cost of stalling on every branch grow with newer, deeper pipelines?
options: Branch targets become unknown after retirement
Deeper pipelines cannot use a fetch PC
Deeper pipelines have fewer branch instructions
More stages lie between fetch and branch resolution, so more cycles are idle per branch
quiz.explanation: Direction and target are resolved at decode or execute, so the idle or wasted stages scale with the distance from fetch to resolution.

clips.title: Static Prediction: Not-Taken and BTFN
clips.hook: Why always-not-taken fails on loops and how backward-taken/forward-not-taken fixes it.
clips.summary: Always-not-taken mispredicts a loop's back-edge n−1 times over n iterations. BTFN predicts backward branches taken (loops) and forward ones not taken (ifs), reaching about 65–80%, but it needs the target early, which is not available at fetch.

quiz.question: Under always-not-taken, how many mispredictions occur for a loop back-edge executed n times (taken n−1 times, then not taken)?
options: n
quiz.explanation: The branch is taken n−1 times, each mispredicted as not taken; the final not-taken is correct.

clips.title: 1-bit vs 2-bit Saturating Counter Predictors
clips.hook: Why a 1-bit predictor mispredicts twice per inner-loop run and how a 2-bit counter adds hysteresis.
clips.summary: A 1-bit history table remembers the last outcome per branch, so a nested inner loop causes two mispredictions per run: at loop exit and at the next first iteration. A 2-bit saturating counter (0–1 not taken, 2–3 taken) needs two consecutive wrong outcomes to flip, raising accuracy to about 90–94%.

quiz.question: Why does a 2-bit saturating counter beat a 1-bit predictor on a nested inner loop?
options: It uses global history
It is a static rule
One loop-exit outcome does not flip the prediction, so the next run's first iteration is still predicted taken
It stores the branch target
quiz.explanation: Hysteresis means a single not-taken at loop exit moves the counter only from strongly to weakly taken, so the prediction stays taken.

clips.title: Polyak Momentum: Velocity as Smoothing and Acceleration
clips.hook: How a velocity term makes SGD less sensitive to learning rate and smooths stochastic noise.
clips.summary: Momentum keeps a velocity state; rho sets resistance to change and the learning rate sets the gradient's impulse. Consistent gradient directions build velocity, enabling faster progress, hopping small troughs, and damping stochastic noise, though overshoot is still possible.
clips.videoTitle: Optimization for Deep Learning (Momentum, RMSprop, AdaGrad, Adam)

quiz.question: In SGD with momentum, what is the effect when gradients point in a consistent direction across many steps?
options: Velocity accumulates, so the weights cover more distance per step
The learning rate is decayed automatically
Each parameter gets a separate learning rate
The gradient is computed at a look-ahead point
quiz.explanation: Velocity is a running accumulation of gradients, so consistent directions build it up and speed progress while noisy directions average out.

clips.title: Nesterov Momentum: Gradient at the Look-Ahead Point
clips.hook: The one change separating Nesterov from classical momentum and why it helps.
clips.summary: Nesterov evaluates the gradient after applying the velocity jump, at the look-ahead position, instead of at the current position. The gradient at the old position may be inappropriate after the velocity move, so the look-ahead gradient corrects for this.
clips.videoTitle: Optimization for Deep Learning (Momentum, RMSprop, AdaGrad, Adam)

quiz.question: What distinguishes Nesterov momentum from classical momentum?
options: It uses a separate learning rate per weight
It removes the velocity term
The gradient is evaluated at the position after the velocity jump
It divides by the root of accumulated squared gradients
quiz.explanation: Nesterov computes the gradient at w plus the velocity jump (look-ahead), so the correction reflects where the weights are about to be.

clips.title: RMSprop and Adam: Decaying Averages, Momentum, Bias Correction
clips.hook: Exponential averaging fixes AdaGrad's decay, and Adam adds momentum plus bias correction.
clips.summary: RMSprop replaces AdaGrad's sum with an exponentially discounted average (beta), so the effective rate can both fall and rise. Adam combines this with a momentum term m, and corrects the zero-initialisation bias of m and v by dividing by 1 minus beta^t, which matters most early on.
clips.videoTitle: Optimization for Deep Learning (Momentum, RMSprop, AdaGrad, Adam)

quiz.question: Why does Adam divide m and v by (1 - beta^t)?
options: To counter the bias toward zero from initialising m and v at zero
To avoid division by zero
To make the learning rate decay over time
To implement the Nesterov look-ahead
quiz.explanation: Zero-initialised exponential averages are biased low early on; dividing by 1 - beta^t corrects this, and the correction fades as t grows.

clips.title: Carrying Control and Destination Register Down the Pipe
clips.hook: Why pipeline registers must carry the destination register ID and write-enable to write-back.
clips.summary: An instruction moves on, so everything it needs later, such as the destination register ID and the control signals, must travel with it in the pipeline registers. Taking the write register from the decode stage's current instruction instead is a bug. Also, ALU ops still traverse the memory stage to keep timing uniform, which wastes time and avoids write-back conflicts.
clips.videoTitle: Design of Digital Circuits - Lecture 14: Pipelining (ETH Zürich, Spring 2018)

quiz.question: Why must the destination register ID be carried through pipeline registers to write-back?
options: Because the register file has only one write port
Because by write-back the decode stage holds a different, younger instruction
Because loads have longer latency
To save control logic in the ALU
quiz.explanation: The register-ID field in the decode stage belongs to a younger instruction by then, so the correct destination must travel with the instruction.

clips.title: Pipeline Control: Decode Once vs Decode Locally
clips.hook: Two ways to supply stage-specific control signals, and their trade-offs.
clips.summary: One option is to decode once in the decode stage and buffer the control signals in pipeline registers, dropping each signal after its stage consumes it. The other is to carry the instruction fields and decode locally in each stage. The first costs wider registers, the second costs more distributed combinational logic, so the choice depends on the design.
clips.videoTitle: Design of Digital Circuits - Lecture 14: Pipelining (ETH Zürich, Spring 2018)

quiz.question: What is the main trade-off between decoding control once and decoding locally per stage?
options: Fewer stages versus more stages
Correctness versus speed
Forwarding versus stalling
Wider pipeline registers versus more distributed decode logic
quiz.explanation: Decoding once buffers many control bits in the registers. Local decoding carries fewer bits but replicates decode logic.

clips.title: Why Real Pipelines Violate All Ideal Assumptions
clips.hook: External fragmentation, internal fragmentation, and dependencies, each hurting performance differently.
clips.summary: Different instructions do not need all stages, which causes external fragmentation. Stages with unequal latency under one clock cause internal fragmentation. Inter-instruction dependences force stalls and need detection to keep results correct.
clips.videoTitle: Design of Digital Circuits - Lecture 14: Pipelining (ETH Zürich, Spring 2018)

quiz.question: What is internal fragmentation in a pipeline?
options: Cache lines partly filled
Stages finishing early but still taking a full clock cycle
Registers split across stages
Stages idle because an instruction does not need them
quiz.explanation: Internal fragmentation comes from unequal stage delays under a common clock. External fragmentation is an instruction skipping a stage.

clips.title: Resource Contention: Duplicate, Multi-Port, or Stall
clips.hook: Structural hazards and why to prioritize the later stage when stalling.
clips.summary: Contention can be removed by duplicating the resource (split I/D memories or caches) or by adding ports. The alternative is to stall one stage, which suits rarely used resources such as the shared FPU in Niagra. If a load and a fetch contend for a single memory, stall the earlier stage (fetch), so the older instruction drains.
clips.videoTitle: Design of Digital Circuits - Lecture 14: Pipelining (ETH Zürich, Spring 2018)

quiz.question: With one memory port, a load in the memory stage and a fetch contend. Which should stall, and why?
options: The fetch, so the later-stage instruction can leave the pipeline
The load, since it is older
Neither
Both
quiz.explanation: Prioritizing the older instruction lets it drain, and stalling the earlier stage keeps the pipeline making progress.

clips.title: Fetch Problem: Control Dependence and Variable-Length ISAs
clips.hook: Why even the next sequential PC is unknown at fetch in variable-length ISAs.
clips.summary: Control dependence is a data dependence on the PC. At fetch you don't yet know whether the instruction is a branch, so you predict. With variable-length ISAs like x86 you cannot even compute the next sequential address until decode reveals the instruction length.
clips.videoTitle: Design of Digital Circuits - Lecture 14: Pipelining (ETH Zürich, Spring 2018)

quiz.question: Why is the next sequential PC hard to compute in x86 pipelines?
options: Branches are always taken
Instruction length is known only after decode
The PC register is shared
Memory is slow
quiz.explanation: Instructions are 1 to 17 bytes, so the length of the current instruction, which is needed for the next address, comes from decode.

clips.title: Implementing Stalls and Bubbles in Hardware
clips.hook: Disable PC and IR writes, inject a bubble, and why a valid bit beats a NOP encoding.
clips.summary: To stall, disable writes to the PC and the fetch/decode registers so the stalled instruction stays put, and inject a bubble into the next stage. A bubble can be a cleared valid bit or NOP-like control signals. A valid bit is more testable and debuggable.
clips.videoTitle: Design of Digital Circuits - Lecture 14: Pipelining (ETH Zürich, Spring 2018)

clips.title: Data Forwarding and Why Load-Use Still Stalls
clips.hook: Forwarding muxes, priority for the youngest producer, and the load-use limit.
clips.summary: Forwarding adds bypass paths from the memory and write-back stages into the ALU input muxes, with comparators choosing the source. If both match, the younger instruction's value wins. A load-use dependence cannot be forwarded without lengthening the cycle, since memory and ALU delays would chain, so a stall is needed.
clips.videoTitle: Design of Digital Circuits - Lecture 14: Pipelining (ETH Zürich, Spring 2018)

quiz.question: Why can't a load's data be forwarded to a dependent ALU instruction with no stall?
options: Loads don't write registers
Forwarding works only for branches
The register file is busy
It would put memory access and ALU in one cycle, lengthening the clock
quiz.explanation: Load data appears at the end of the memory stage, so using it in the very next ALU stage would chain both delays in one cycle.

clips.title: Writing swap and the Rule of Three
clips.hook: The `using std::swap` plus unqualified call pattern for ADL, and why the destructor, copy ctor and copy assignment go together.
clips.summary: A member swap does `using std::swap;` and then makes unqualified calls so ADL finds type-specific swaps. If you need a custom destructor, copy constructor or copy assignment, you almost certainly need all three.
clips.videoTitle: Back To Basics: The Special Member Functions - Klaus Iglberger - CppCon 2021

quiz.question: Why call `swap(a, b)` unqualified after `using std::swap;` in a swap implementation?
options: It avoids a move
It is faster than `std::swap`
It is required by the standard for noexcept
It lets ADL find a better swap for the member's type while still falling back to std::swap
quiz.explanation: Unqualified lookup with ADL finds a type-specific swap in the type's namespace, and the using-declaration provides the std fallback.

clips.title: Rule of Zero via unique_ptr and shared_ptr
clips.hook: Replace a raw owning pointer with a smart pointer and note how the class semantics change.
clips.summary: A unique_ptr removes the need for a destructor but makes the class non-copyable, so copy operations must still be written. A shared_ptr gives the Rule of Zero but changes the semantics from exclusive to shared ownership.
clips.videoTitle: Back To Basics: The Special Member Functions - Klaus Iglberger - CppCon 2021

quiz.question: Why is replacing an owning `T*` with `shared_ptr<T>` not a pure refactoring to the Rule of Zero?
options: It requires a virtual destructor
Copies now share one resource instead of each owning its own
It disables move
shared_ptr cannot be destroyed
quiz.explanation: Copying a widget now shares the resource, which differs from the deep-copy semantics of the original.

clips.title: Deleted vs absent move: Rule of Three vs Five
clips.hook: `= delete` on move is not the same as not declaring it. Absent move falls back to copy.
clips.summary: A deleted function still takes part in overload resolution and gives an error if selected. An undeclared move lets rvalues fall back to copy. So follow the Rule of Five when you want to control move, and the Rule of Three when copy fallback is intended.
clips.videoTitle: Back To Basics: The Special Member Functions - Klaus Iglberger - CppCon 2021

quiz.question: A class declares a copy constructor and destructor but no move operations. What does `Widget b = std::move(a);` do?
options: Compile error
Undefined behavior
Calls an implicit move
Calls the copy constructor
quiz.explanation: Move is not declared, so the rvalue binds to const Widget& and the copy constructor runs. If move were `= delete`, it would be a compile error.

clips.title: Double Descent and the Interpolation Threshold
clips.hook: Why test risk peaks where parameters ≈ data points, then falls again as capacity grows.
clips.summary: The classical U-shaped risk curve is incomplete: at the interpolation threshold (parameters ≈ data points) test risk peaks, and beyond it test risk decreases again while training risk stays near zero. This effect is not due to regularization, which would reduce effective complexity instead.
clips.videoTitle: Reconciling modern machine learning and the bias-variance trade-off

quiz.question: In the double-descent picture, what happens to training and test risk beyond the interpolation threshold?
options: Training risk rises while test risk falls
Training risk stays near zero while test risk decreases again
Test risk stays at its peak value
Both training and test risk rise
quiz.explanation: Past the threshold models interpolate the training data (near-zero training risk), yet test risk falls again, giving the second descent.

clips.title: Low-Norm Interpolation as Implicit Inductive Bias
clips.hook: Why overparameterized models that interpolate can still generalize: smoothness via minimum norm.
clips.summary: With many parameters, a model can interpolate training data using a low-norm, smooth function rather than a wildly oscillating one. Optimizers like SGD tend to find low-norm solutions, and that smoothness explains good behavior between training points.
clips.videoTitle: Reconciling modern machine learning and the bias-variance trade-off

quiz.question: Why can an interpolating overparameterized model generalize well according to the paper's explanation?
options: It uses fewer effective parameters via explicit regularization
Training error being zero guarantees low test error
The inductive bias selects a low-norm, smooth interpolant
Noise is removed from the training data
quiz.explanation: Among many interpolating functions, a low-norm one is smooth between data points, which helps generalization.
